title: My Leader Only Gets Sound Bites About My Performance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece addresses the reality that in flat, span-heavy organizations, leaders form their view of a team member's performance primarily from fragments—chat threads, sidebar comments, overheard snippets—rather than from comprehensive observation. The author argues that the gap between what a team member actually accomplishes and how their leader perceives it is one of the most underrated career risks. The instinctive response—more status reports and one-on-ones—provides limited leverage because leaders trust self-generated updates less than secondhand reports. The real strategy is managing sideways: making peers' and clients' successes visible so they return the favor, giving credit generously and specifically so colleagues become a PR team, and asking directly when someone offers a compliment whether they would share it with your leader. The article reframes perception management as a professional responsibility rather than vanity: work only speaks when someone chooses to listen, and a leader's finite attention is competed for by everyone around you. The high performers' advantage is not just doing excellent work but designing the sound bites through which that work gets compressed and communicated.
points: In flat organizations with large spans of control, leaders increasingly form their view of team members through fragments—chat threads, sidebar comments, and overheard snippets—making the gap between actual performance and perceived performance one of the most underrated career risks.

Leaders trust secondhand reports far more than self-generated updates, because they assume personal updates are self-serving—meaning managing sideways (through peers and clients) generates more credibility than managing up directly.
Making others' successes visible and giving credit generously are the engines of reciprocal recognition: colleagues who receive public credit tend to return it without being asked.

Asking someone who has just complimented your work to share that compliment with your leader is not self-serving—it simply extends praise the person already wanted to give, and most people are delighted to do so.

Perception management is not vanity but a professional responsibility: work only speaks when someone chooses to listen, and the high performer's job is to design the sound bite that best represents the real work being done.
quotes: As organizations get flatter and leaders manage an increasing number of team members, staying abreast of everyone's successes and progress has become a significant challenge.
The gap between what a team member gets done and how their leader perceives that work is one of the most underrated risks in a career.

Leaders trust secondhand reports far more than self-generated ones, because they assume a personal update is self-serving. When a peer mentions in a meeting that you were the one who caught a critical mistake, or a client describes how invaluable your influence has become, that sound bite does more to promote your work than ten status reports.
The real strategy, then, isn't just managing up but managing sideways so well that other people become your PR team.
The easiest version goes something like this: 'That means a lot. Would you mind mentioning it to my leader?'

Perception management is not vanity. It's part of the job. Many high performers, especially junior ones, secretly reject the idea of shaping how they are seen, believing the work should speak for itself. It doesn't.
